moduleSummaries.module: Labels container API surface (Labels.swift, LazyFrameList.swift, LazyDataStore.swift) + LabelsSet
moduleSummaries.summary: The Swift `Labels` is a thin (~384-line) container covering frame storage (eager + lazy/LazyFrameList), basic queries (`frame(for:at:)`, `frames(for:)`, `instances(for:)`), a few structural mutators (`addFrame`, `removeFrame`, `clearPredictions`, `removeTrack`, `merge`), `materialize`, tensor export via a separate `TensorCodec`, and `DictionaryCodec`. Python (4034 lines) and JS (2696 lines) expose a vastly larger surface: rich `__getitem__`/`find` with foreign-video resolution, `numpy`/`from_numpy`/`update_from_numpy`, `clean`/`remove_predictions`/`extract`/`split`/`make_training_splits`/`trim`, full skeleton node management (`rename_nodes`/`remove_nodes`/`reorder_nodes`/`replace_skeleton`), video management (`add_video`/`replace_videos`/`replace_filenames`/`match_video`/`apply_crops`), per-annotation query families (`get_rois`/`get_masks`/`get_bboxes`/`get_centroids`/`get_label_images`), matcher-based `merge`/`match` with `MergeResult`/`MatchResult`/provenance history, cached frame/track indices (`get_frame`/`get_track_annotations`/`reindex`), the `n_user_instances`/`n_pred_instances`/`n_frames_per_video`/`n_instances_per_track` counts, `copy`, and the entire `LabelsSet` container. Most of these are absent in Swift. For a SwiftUI annotation GUI the highest-priority gaps are O(1) frame/track lookup, foreign-video resolution, skeleton/video editing wrappers, `clean`/`remove_predictions`, annotation query families, `copy`, suggestion/track management, and the `numpy`/`from_numpy` round-trip for the training backend. The Swift `merge` is present but a simplified identity-only version that diverges substantially from the canonical matcher-driven pipeline.

moduleSummaries.module: Instance / PredictedInstance / LabeledFrame model + Point/PointsArray + bbox/centroid/identity types
moduleSummaries.summary: The Swift port has the skeleton of the model layer (Instance, PredictedInstance, LabeledFrame, Point, PointsArray, Track) with correct identity semantics and an efficient interleaved-Float32 PointsArray, but it is missing the large majority of the behavioral surface present in Python and JS. Critically absent are numpy()-equivalent accessors on Instance/PredictedInstance/LabeledFrame, n_visible/is_empty/centroid_xy, update_skeleton/replace_skeleton, from_numpy/empty/dict+array constructors, and IoU/pose/identity comparison helpers — all of which the Python and JS ports implement fully. LabeledFrame.merge() is a simplified stub that does not perform spatial matching, return conflicts, merge frame-level annotations, or resolve is_negative; it also lacks remove_empty_instances, remove_predictions, unused_predictions, append, matches, and the centroids/bboxes/masks/rois/label_images annotation containers entirely. Three first-class annotation type hierarchies — Centroid, BoundingBox, and Identity — plus the 3D pose types (Instance3D/PredictedInstance3D) have no Swift equivalent at all. The GUI north star is most blocked by missing numpy/centroid/bbox accessors (rendering overlays, selection hit-testing), the real merge cascade (proofreading workflows), update/replace_skeleton (skeleton editing), and the annotation containers; the backend is most blocked by numpy(invisible_as_nan), per-instance numpy with scores, and from_numpy round-tripping.

moduleSummaries.module: Skeleton / Node / Edge / Symmetry model + skeleton JSON/YAML/SLP codecs + Video model
moduleSummaries.summary: The Swift Skeleton model covers the core mutation surface (addNode/removeNode with instance migration, addEdge, addSymmetry, O(1) name/index lookup, identity equality) and even adds GUI-friendly migrating variants Python/JS lack. But it is missing the entire derived-accessor surface Python exposes for training/inference and matching: node_names, edge_inds, edge_names, symmetry_inds/symmetry_names, get_flipped_node_inds, require_node, rename_node(s), reorder_nodes, match_nodes/matches/node_similarities, name/int indexing, __contains__, and the bulk add_* helpers. The SLP skeleton codec (SkeletonCodec.encodeToNetworkX/decodeFromNetworkX) diverges materially from Python's SkeletonSLPEncoder/SkeletonSLPDecoder: it embeds full py/state node objects instead of integer node indices, uses a string "type":"BODY" instead of the jsonpickle EdgeType py/reduce/py/id scheme, encodes symmetries in a non-standard "graph.symmetries" array rather than type-2 links, and omits the global node-superset dicts — so round-trip fidelity with real .slp files and other SLEAP tools is at risk. There is no standalone skeleton JSON (jsonpickle) codec, no training-config detection, and no YAML codec at all. The Video model is a thin identity stub: it has filename/sourceVideo/backendType/backendMetadata/frameCount/frameSize but lacks shape, grayscale, exists, open/close, is_open, from_filename, replace_filename, original_video, fps, and the whole matches_*/dedup/merge/crop family present in both Python and JS.

This is the weakest-parity area of the Swift port. The ENTIRE matching/merge subsystem (matching.py / matching.ts, ~1900 LOC) is absent: no SkeletonMatcher/InstanceMatcher/TrackMatcher/VideoMatcher, no match-method enums, no MergeResult/MatchResult/ConflictResolution/MergeError, no FrameStrategy, and the supporting model methods (Skeleton.matches, Skeleton.node_similarities, Instance.same_pose_as/same_identity_as/overlaps_with, Track.matches, Video.matches_path/content/shape) are not implemented. Swift's only merge is a coarse identity-keyed LabeledFrame.merge with a 6-case enum that does NO spatial/IoU instance matching, returns no result/conflict objects, and does no video/skeleton/track correspondence — it is not behaviorally compatible with upstream. ROI, SegmentationMask, and SuggestionFrame exist but as simplified single-struct value types that diverge from upstream's abstract User/Predicted class hierarchy, drop most geometry operations, and (for ROI/mask) carry no WKB or scale/offset support. LabelImage (dense integer per-pixel segmentation, label_image.py / label-image.ts) is entirely absent. Note: there is no upstream symbol literally named "MatchedFrame"; the prompt's reference maps to MatchResult/MergeResult plus LabeledFrame.merge — all missing. Suggestion generation is not a library feature in Python or JS (only the SuggestionFrame data type exists), so no generator gap applies.

moduleSummaries.module: SleapHDF5/SLP (SLP HDF5 read/write, lazy/streaming, embedded video, versioning, provenance, sessions/cameras, ROIs/masks)
moduleSummaries.summary: Swift covers the SLP 1.0-1.5 core well: /frames, /instances, /points, /pred_points compound datasets read+write with field-by-field column reads, lazy column store with LRU cache + on-demand materialization, eager path, embedded-video read (vlen/fixed-length/raw HDF5, PNG/JPEG end detection, channel_order, frame_numbers, source_video JSON), tracks, suggestions (with group), negative_frames, pre-1.1 coordinate adjustment, <1.2 tracking_score gating, from_predicted linking, and basic ROI/mask read+write. However it hard-caps at format 1.5 (`kMaxSupportedFormatVersion`), throwing `formatVersionTooNew` on any file >=1.6 — which current Python writes routinely (1.9 for predicted/instance-linked masks, 2.0 bboxes, 2.1 spatial transforms, 2.3 crops, 2.4 mask provenance). That alone blocks reading most modern projects. Whole annotation families present in Python AND JS are entirely absent in Swift: bounding boxes (/bboxes), centroids (/centroids), label images (/label_images), identities (/identities_json), score maps, and /video_crops. Sessions/cameras are technically present but Swift reads/writes a bespoke `camera_to_video` JSON schema that does NOT match the Python/JS `calibration`+`camcorder_to_video_idx_map`+`frame_group_dicts` format, so multiview round-trips are incompatible and drop all calibration, frame groups, instance groups, and 3D instances. There is no embed-on-save pipeline (embed="all"/"user"/"suggestions"/"source", VideoReferenceMode) — Swift can only copy pre-existing embedded groups or dump an in-memory cache. ROI/mask write also diverges (no predicted variants, no scale/offset/tracking_score/instance/from_predicted columns, no roi_*/mask_* string datasets, no gzip), and provenance is lossily coerced to `[String:String]`.

moduleSummaries.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker
moduleSummaries.summary: All four Swift codecs exist but diverge substantially from the Python reference in format schema, not just feature coverage. Two are functionally broken against real upstream files: the AlphaTracker reader expects an invented schema (image_path/animal_id/keypoints[[x,y]]/confidence) that no real AlphaTracker file uses — Python's actual format is a list of {filename, class:"image", annotations:[{class:"Face"...},{class:"point",x,y}]} objects, so the Swift reader throws unsupportedFormat on every genuine file. The Label Studio codec uses a parentID grouping convention for both read and write instead of Python's rectanglelabels-individuals + relation (from_id/to_id) structure, making Swift LS files non-interoperable with Python in both directions, plus Swift requires an explicit SkeletonMapping where Python infers nodes automatically. The CSV codec implements a completely different format family (long-table video,frame_idx,skeleton,instance,node,x,y,... one-row-per-point) than Python's pandas-DataFrame-backed formats (sleap/dlc/points/instances/frames with auto-detection, metadata sidecar JSON, chunking, DLC delegation) — there is zero format overlap, so neither can read the other's output. COCO is the closest to parity for the keypoints path but omits detection-only ROIs/masks/bboxes, segmentation (polygon + RLE), binary-vs-ternary visibility encoding option, multi-image-shape video grouping, track export via attributes.object_id, panoptic format, image-filename control, and dataset-root path resolution. None of these codecs are exposed via Python-compatible numeric/array export and several edge cases (NaN handling, score semantics, predicted-point scores defaulting to 0) differ.

Across these four converters, the Swift port is materially behind both Python and JS, and in two cases reads/writes the wrong on-disk format entirely. The Swift AnalysisHDF5Codec uses dataset name `locations` with a fixed `(T,N,K,2)` canonical layout, but the real SLEAP analysis format (Python + JS) names it `tracks` and defaults to the MATLAB preset `(n_tracks, 2, n_nodes, n_frames)` with `dims`/`preset` attributes — so the Swift codec cannot read genuine SLEAP analysis files nor produce them, and has none of the preset/axis-ordering machinery, occupancy filtering, or `to_analysis_arrays` untracked slotting. The Swift JABSCodec reads a generic 4D `poseest/points` keyed off a `node_names` attribute and writes a single generic layout; it ignores the real JABS pose-version model (v2 single-mouse 3D, v3 `instance_track_id`+`instance_count`, v4+ `instance_embed_id`, the y/x coordinate flip, the built-in 12-node "Mouse" skeleton with edges+symmetries, and v5 static-object ROIs), so it interoperates with neither Python nor JS JABS files. The Swift DLCCodec reads pandas HDFStore "fixed" HDF5, whereas Python (and only Python — JS has no DLC at all) reads DLC annotation CSVs plus full project/config.yaml/train-test-split support; the two do not read the same files. The Swift YOLOCodec is pose-only, single-class, uses the wrong config filename (`dataset.yaml` vs `data.yaml`), and lacks detection/segmentation tasks, bounding boxes, ROIs, splits, and LabelsSet — features present in both Python and JS.

moduleSummaries.module: io/{geojson, trackmate, seq, tiff, nwb, nwb_annotations, nwb_predictions, leap}
moduleSummaries.summary: None of the six focus-area formats (GeoJSON, TrackMate, SEQ, TIFF/LabelImage, NWB, LEAP .mat) exist in the Swift port — there are no corresponding source files under Sources/, and the model prerequisites are also missing or divergent. Two of these formats are also implemented in the JS port (GeoJSON + TrackMate, plus TIFF label-images), so they are clearly in scope for cross-platform parity; SEQ, NWB, and LEAP are Python-only. The Swift ROI model is a flat [SIMD2<Float>] points struct with no Shapely-equivalent geometry (Polygon/MultiPolygon), no __geo_interface__/toGeoJSON, and no from_polygon/from_box/is_bbox/area/centroid — so even the lightweight GeoJSON path needs both a model upgrade and a codec. The Swift port has no Centroid/PredictedCentroid model (blocking TrackMate) and no LabelImage/from_binary_masks model (blocking TIFF). NWB and LEAP depend on the Python/h5py-only ecosystem (pynwb, ndx-pose, ndx-multisubjects, pymatreader) with no Swift equivalents and are correctly flagged out-of-scope in CLAUDE.md Phase 5; they remain low-priority for an Apple-native GUI/backend.

moduleSummaries.module: Codecs: DictionaryCodec + TensorCodec (numpy/tensor export, dataframe export, skeleton YAML, training-config parsing)
moduleSummaries.summary: The Swift port has a functioning round-trip `DictionaryCodec` (encode/decode Labels) and a `TensorCodec.toTensor` that produces a 4D [frames, tracks, nodes, 2/3] array, but both are significantly simpler than the Python and JS references. The dictionary format diverges structurally from Python/JS (uses keys "frames"/"video"/"skeleton" instead of "labeled_frames"/"video_idx"/"skeleton_idx", and serializes full nested skeleton/edge dicts rather than index references), so it is NOT JSON-interchange-compatible with the canonical format. TensorCodec has two correctness bugs vs Python `to_numpy`: (1) the frame axis is indexed by frameStore position rather than `frame_idx - first_frame` so frame alignment to video timeline is wrong, and (2) all untracked instances collapse into track slot 0, overwriting each other (Python slots them positionally via `untracked=True`). Entirely absent: `from_numpy`/`from_tensor` (array -> Labels), the full `to_analysis_arrays` builder API in SleapIO (occupancy/point_scores/instance_scores/tracking_scores tuples — though SleapHDF5.AnalysisHDF5Codec.write reimplements a partial version), the entire dataframe codec (points/instances/frames/multi_index formats + from_dataframe), skeleton YAML, and training-config skeleton parsing. Backend relevance is high for the numpy fixes and from_numpy; GUI relevance centers on dictionary interchange fidelity and is otherwise low for dataframe/analysis paths.

moduleSummaries.module: SleapRendering (PoseRenderer + Colors + RenderOptions) vs Python sleap_io.rendering / sleap-io.js src/rendering
moduleSummaries.summary: The Swift port has a minimal CoreGraphics pose renderer that draws edges, circle nodes, optional node-name labels, track-name text, and a dashed bounding box, colored only by instance index. It is dramatically behind both Python and JS, which share a rich, feature-complete rendering pipeline: a full color system (resolve_color with hex/named/grayscale/palette-index specs, 9-13 palettes, color_by track/instance/node/auto schemes), five marker shapes, motion trails, segmentation/label-image/ROI/bbox/centroid overlays with per-track coloring, pre/post/per-instance callbacks with world_to_canvas, cropping (pixel + normalized), solid-color backgrounds, single-image and full video rendering with ffmpeg/skia, and image/PNG/JPEG export. For a SwiftUI sleap-label replacement the highest-value missing pieces are color_by="track" coloring (consistency across frames is essential for track editing), marker shapes, score/visibility-aware node styling, ROI/mask/centroid overlays (these models exist in Swift but aren't drawn), and a SwiftUI-friendly render-into-context API; trails, callbacks, cropping, and video export are secondary. The backend (sleap.swift) needs almost none of this except possibly headless frame compositing for QC montages.

The Python reference implements a full composable transform stack: a `Transform` dataclass with a fixed crop→scale→rotate→pad→flip pipeline, a `to_matrix()`/`output_size()`/`apply_to_points()`/`apply_to_frame()` API, standalone frame ops (crop/scale/rotate/flip/pad with PIL interpolation and OOB fill), standalone point ops (crop/uncrop/scale/rotate/pad + OOB masks), CLI parsers (parse_scale/resolve_scale/parse_crop/parse_pad), and a video/labels pipeline (transform_video, transform_embedded_video, transform_labels, compute_transform_summary). The JavaScript port is intentionally minimal — only the crop subset for SLP 2.3 virtual cropping (cropFrame, cropPoints, uncropPoints) — and omits scale/rotate/pad/flip entirely. Our Swift port sits in between: it has a low-level affine matrix toolkit (AffineTransform2D: identity/translation/scale/rotation/compose) and Instance-level convenience methods (translated/scaled/rotated/cropped/transformed) plus an Accelerate-backed PointsArray.apply(transform:), but it has NO unified Transform type, NO flip, NO pad, NO crop-coordinate offsetting helper, NO frame/image transforms, NO output_size/to_matrix pipeline, NO OOB visibility marking, and NO video/labels-level transform pipeline. For the GUI north star the affine + Instance helpers cover live point editing overlays, but a from-scratch Transform pipeline (especially crop offsetting for virtual crop and flip/rotate around image center with correct center-pixel indexing) would be needed for an augmentation/export feature.

moduleSummaries.module: SleapVideo — Video read/write backends (media, HDF5 embedded, image sequence, SEQ, TIFF, streaming, crop, frame cache, grayscale, channel order, seeking)
moduleSummaries.summary: The Swift port covers the three highest-value read paths for a GUI — AVFoundation media video, an HDF5 embedded-frame backend (in SleapHDF5), and an image-sequence directory backend — plus a per-Video NSCache frame cache and exact/adaptive seek tolerance. Those three are reasonably close to behavioral parity for display. Everything beyond that is missing: there is no grayscale autodetection or forced-grayscale collapse, no Norpix .seq backend, no multi-page/rank-3/rank-4 TiffVideo, no CropVideoBackend, no HDF5 channels_first input_format, no HDF5 crop-pushdown, no streaming/range-request HDF5 reader, and no video writer at all (VideoWriter/MJPEGFrameWriter). The Swift VideoBackend protocol also returns CGImage rather than raw pixel arrays, which means there is no numpy()-equivalent frame-tensor path and grayscale/channel semantics are baked into CGImage RGBA, diverging from Python's (H,W,C) ndarray contract. Channel-order (BGR/RGB) handling for embedded frames is present and faithful; FPS is read for media but never for embedded/seq sources. For unblocking a SwiftUI annotation GUI, the most impactful gaps are grayscale handling, the .seq backend, and TIFF stacks (all are real inputs in behavioral neuroscience labs); for a training backend the missing raw-array frame export and crop-pushdown matter most.

moduleSummaries.module: io/main.py (load_file/save_file dispatch + load_*/save_* family) and io/cli.py (sio CLI) vs Swift LabelsIO + SleapioCLI
moduleSummaries.summary: Python's io/main.py is a large dispatch hub: load_file/save_file auto-detect 13+ formats (slp, nwb, leap/.mat, json -> alphatracker/coco/labelstudio by content-sniff, .h5 -> analysis_h5/jabs by content, geojson, dlc/dlc_project, csv -> trackmate/dlc/csv by content, ultralytics dir, video by extension), with parallel load_slp/save_slp keyword-rich entry points, a remote URL/Google-Drive layer, and helpers (load_skeleton, save_skeleton, load_labels_set, load_label_images, load_video). The JS port (main.ts) covers a much smaller surface: loadSlp/saveSlp (with browser-Worker streaming), loadAnalysisH5/saveAnalysisH5, loadSlpSet/saveSlpSet, loadVideo, isAnalysisH5File, and TIFF label-image readers; it has NO load_file/save_file unified dispatcher. The Swift port's Labels.load/save (LabelsIO.swift) + inferLoadFormat/inferSaveFormat dispatch over a FileFormat enum of 9 formats (slp, cocoJSON, csv, labelStudio, yolo, alphaTracker, analysisHDF5, jabs, deepLabCut) and content-sniff JSON/HDF5; its CLI (SleapioCLI: info/show/convert) is a thin subset of Python's 18-command sio. Major Swift gaps vs Python: no NWB/LEAP/TrackMate/Ultralytics/GeoJSON formats; no .mat/.nwb/.geojson/video/.yaml dispatch; no load_video/load_skeleton/load_labels_set/load_label_images; no remote URL loading; and the CLI is missing 15 of 18 commands (export, split/unsplit, merge, filenames, render, fix, embed/unembed, trim, reencode, apply-crops, transform). Most missing formats (NWB/LEAP) are out of scope on Apple, but the missing CLI commands and load_video dispatch are GUI-relevant.

gaps.description: Python _read_labels_lazy_from_open_file (slp.py:3097-3143) builds per-frame annotation dicts and synthesizes non-lazy supplementary LabeledFrames for (video,frame) keys that have annotations but no /frames row, plus keeps undistributed annotations (video=-1/frame=-1) in separate buckets. Swift attaches ROIs/masks to Labels.rois/masks as flat lists with index fields but never creates frames for annotation-only entries nor distinguishes undistributed.

gaps.module: SleapHDF5/SLP (SLP HDF5 read/write, lazy/streaming, embedded video, versioning, provenance, sessions/cameras, ROIs/masks)

gaps.description: Python parses a top-level JSON array of frame objects each with filename, class:"image", and annotations[] where class:"Face" begins a new instance and subsequent class:"point" entries (with numeric x,y) are its keypoints. Node count is inferred as the max points following any Face; nodes are named "1","2",...; all images become one ImageVideo. Swift's reader instead expects a totally different/invented schema (image_path, animal_id, keypoints as [[x,y]], confidence) that does not exist in any real AlphaTracker export.
gaps.notes: This is the single most severe gap: Swift AlphaTrackerCodec.read throws SleapIOError.unsupportedFormat on EVERY genuine AlphaTracker file, and FileFormat sniffing keys on image_path/animal_id/keypoints which real files never contain, so auto-detect also fails. Effectively the AlphaTracker import is non-functional. Python has no write side either, so Swift correctly omits write. Low GUI/backend relevance (niche import format) but high correctness defect.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.feature: alphatracker node naming + skeleton inference (1-based string names, ragged frames)
gaps.description: Python scans ALL frames to find max points-per-Face and names nodes "1".."N"; pads instances shorter than N with NaN. Swift derives nodeCount only from the FIRST entry's keypoints length and names nodes "node_0".. (or a Config override), so ragged frames and node-name parity are wrong even if the schema were fixed.
gaps.notes: Subsumed by fixing the schema gap above but listed separately because node naming convention ("1".. vs "node_0"..) and multi-frame max-scan are distinct behaviors.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.description: Python multi-animal grouping uses rectanglelabels results as individuals plus relation results (type:"relation", from_id/to_id, direction) to attach keypointlabels to a given individual (filter_and_index + build_relation_map). Leftover keypoints become a single extra instance. Swift instead groups keypoint results by a non-standard parentID field. Real Label Studio exports do not carry parentID, so Swift read groups all keypoints into one instance per result-id (single-animal collapse) for genuine files.
gaps.notes: Swift read also can't reconstruct multi-animal instances from real LS files. Cross-implementation interoperability is broken. Mark low GUI relevance only because LS is an external annotation tool, not the native GUI itself; but if importing existing LS projects is a workflow, raise to medium.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.feature: labelstudio write_labels — rectanglelabels bbox + relation links + meta.video block
gaps.description: Python writes, per instance, a rectanglelabels result (full-frame bbox tagged instance_class) plus per-point keypointlabels results plus relation results linking each point id to the instance id; coordinates are percentage x/y = coord/dim*100; it emits a meta.video block {filename, frame_idx, shape}, created_at/updated_at timestamps, was_cancelled/ground_truth/lead_time fields, and skips NaN points. Swift emits keypointlabels with a parentID and value.original_width/height, an id and data.image (basename only), and no rectanglelabels/relation/meta.video/timestamps. Predicted instances go to a "predictions" array (Python has no predictions concept here).
gaps.notes: Round-trip even within Swift works (its read matches its write via parentID), but Swift output is NOT a valid multi-animal Label Studio file and Python cannot reconstruct individuals from it. Also Python's read recovers Video via meta.video (filename+shape+frame_idx); Swift relies on data.image filename and frameIndex always 0, losing video shape and frame index.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.feature: labelstudio automatic node inference (infer_nodes) and skeleton:list/Skeleton overload
gaps.description: Python read_labels accepts skeleton as None (auto-infers node set by scanning all keypointlabels values across tasks), a list[str], or a Skeleton. Swift mandates an explicit SkeletonMapping(labelToNode) and throws invalidSkeleton on empty mapping, so zero-config import is impossible.
gaps.notes: Swift's explicit mapping is arguably a deliberate design choice (noted in its docstring) but it diverges from Python's no-skeleton default path. Low priority for native GUI.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.feature: labelstudio completions key fallback + multiple-annotations warning
gaps.description: Python accepts both "annotations" and legacy "completions" keys and warns when a task has >1 annotation (taking only the first). Swift only reads "annotations" (+ a non-Python "predictions" array) and silently iterates all annotations.
gaps.notes: Minor compatibility gap for older Label Studio exports.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.feature: csv format family: sleap / dlc / points / instances / frames + auto-detect
gaps.description: Python csv.read_labels/write_labels support five formats via a format= param ("auto","sleap","dlc","points","instances","frames") with detect_csv_format() sniffing headers, all backed by the codecs.dataframe to_dataframe/from_dataframe machinery. The default "sleap" Analysis CSV has columns track,frame_idx,instance.score,{node}.x,{node}.y,{node}.score (one row per instance). Swift implements ONE proprietary long-table layout (video,frame_idx,skeleton,instance,node,x,y,visible,complete,track,instance_type,instance_score,point_score,tracking_score; one row per point) with no format param, no detection, and no compatibility with any Python CSV. Neither can read the other's output.
gaps.notes: This is the largest structural gap. backendRelevance high because Export Analysis CSV (sleap format) is the canonical analysis hand-off used by sleap.swift and downstream tooling, and DLC/instances/frames feed numpy-style pipelines. Requires a DataFrame-equivalent abstraction in Swift (no pandas). The bespoke Swift format is internally round-trip-safe but not upstream-compatible.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.feature: csv DLC multi-header read/write (_read_dlc/_write_dlc, scorer, multi/single-animal)
gaps.swiftLocation: n/a (no DLC CSV support in CSVCodec; separate DLC HDF5 path exists elsewhere)
gaps.description: Python write_dlc builds a 3-row (scorer/bodyparts/coords) or 4-row (scorer/individuals/bodyparts/coords) MultiIndex header with image-path row index labeled-data/<video>/img####.png, x/y/likelihood columns gated by include_score, multi-animal when >1 track. read delegates to io.dlc.load_dlc. Swift has no DLC CSV reader/writer in this codec.
gaps.notes: Swift may have DLC HDF5 support under Phase 4; confirm whether DLC CSV specifically is covered. The scorer= and individuals naming are needed for DeepLabCut interop.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.description: Python write_labels(save_metadata=True) writes a sibling .json capturing version, videos (filename+backend_metadata incl shape/fps), skeletons (nodes+edges+symmetries), tracks, suggestions (video_idx+frame_idx), and provenance; read_labels auto-loads it to restore edges, symmetries, suggestions, video shape, and provenance that CSV cannot hold. Swift CSV has no metadata sidecar, so edges/symmetries/suggestions/provenance/video-shape are lost on its CSV round-trip.
gaps.notes: Relevant to GUI project save/restore fidelity if CSV is ever used as an interchange; medium because SLP is the primary GUI format.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.feature: csv write options: include_score, include_empty/all_frames, start_frame/end_frame, chunk_size, video_id, scorer, video filter
gaps.description: Python write_labels exposes include_score, include_empty (pads empty frames with NaN), start_frame/end_frame range, chunk_size for memory-efficient incremental writes, video filter (Video|int), scorer name, and video_id in {path,index,name}. Swift CSVCodec.write takes only (labels, path) with a fixed column set and no filtering/ranging/chunking.

gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

It also attaches bbox/segmentation alongside keypoint instances. Swift requires annotations to have keypoints of length 3*nodeCount and throws corruptData otherwise; it ignores bbox, segmentation, area, iscrowd entirely and has no ROI/mask/bbox model wiring.
gaps.notes: Depends on whether SleapIO has ROI/SegmentationMask/BoundingBox models (CLAUDE.md lists ROI/SegmentationMask structs; bbox model presence unknown). GUI relevance medium if detection overlays / segmentation masks are shown. Swift's strict-length check will reject mixed datasets that Python loads.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.description: Python encodes/decodes COCO column-major (Fortran-order) RLE masks and writes polygon segmentation from ROI exterior coords with bbox/area/iscrowd=1. Swift has no RLE or polygon segmentation support in either direction.
gaps.notes: Pairs with the detection-only gap. Apple-platform note: numpy reshape/transpose must be reimplemented manually but is feasible.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

Swift COCOCodec ignores tracks entirely on both read and write, so multi-animal identity is lost through COCO.

gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.feature: coco visibility_encoding option (binary vs ternary) on read and write
gaps.description: Python encode_keypoints/write_labels accept visibility_encoding="binary"|"ternary" (binary: visible->1/not->0; ternary: visible->2/occluded->1/unlabeled->0). decode_keypoints documents binary-vs-ternary ambiguity. Swift hardcodes a ternary-like scheme with no option, and its read treats v==1 as not-visible (occluded) which conflicts with binary-encoded files where 1 means visible.
gaps.notes: Edge case but affects datasets exported in binary visibility (e.g., some mmpose configs).
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

Swift creates a separate single-frame Video per image (frameIndex 0), does no path resolution, has no dataset_root/grayscale, and does not skip missing images.
gaps.notes: Affects how a GUI would treat a COCO dataset as navigable image sequences vs N isolated videos. Lower priority than detection/track gaps.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.notes: backendRelevance medium for training dataset splits.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.feature: coco write image_filenames control + filename generation from video/frame_idx
gaps.description: Python convert_labels/write_labels accept image_filenames (str or list matching frame count) and otherwise generate per-frame names (image-sequence basename, or <video_stem>_frame_%06d.png for videos). Swift always writes video.filename directly and assumes one frame per video, so multi-frame videos collide on file_name and frame indices are not encoded.
gaps.notes: Round-trip fidelity issue for video-derived COCO exports.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.feature: coco predicted point scores (per-keypoint score round-trip)
gaps.description: Python uses Instance.from_numpy for keypoints (no per-point score in COCO keypoints, which is expected) and stores instance-level score. Swift, when a top-level annotation "score" is present, builds a PredictedInstance with per-point scores hardcoded to 0.0 and instance score from "score". This matches Python's lack of per-point scores but the visibility/score semantics for predicted COCO instances differ subtly (Python keeps the instance a user Instance unless... actually Python COCO never creates PredictedInstance for keypoint annotations; it only does so for detection bboxes). Swift creates PredictedInstance for any keypoint annotation carrying a score, diverging from Python which keeps keypoint annotations as user Instances.
gaps.notes: Behavioral divergence: a COCO keypoint annotation with a top-level score becomes a PredictedInstance in Swift but a user Instance in Python. Affects instance-type fidelity.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.description: Python reads/writes COCO panoptic segmentation: per-frame RGB PNG label images (id = R + G*256 + B*65536), segments_info with category_id/area/bbox/iscrowd, isthing-based Track assignment, into UserLabelImage/LabelImage.Info objects. Swift has no LabelImage model or panoptic support.
gaps.notes: Out of scope for a keypoint annotation GUI; requires PNG label-image encode/decode (PIL-equivalent via CoreGraphics). Low relevance.
gaps.module: Import/Export Codecs: COCO, CSV, Label Studio, AlphaTracker

gaps.swiftLocation: AnalysisHDF5Codec.read(from:) — reads `locations`, falls back to `tracks` only for track NAMES
gaps.description: Python/JS read the 4D pose array from the `tracks` dataset and recover axis order from each dataset's `dims` JSON attribute (or legacy `transpose` attr), supporting matlab/standard/custom orderings. Swift instead reads a dataset literally named `locations` in fixed (T,N,K,2) order with no `dims` handling, and confusingly treats a `tracks` dataset as the track-NAMES string array. Swift cannot read a real sleap-io analysis .h5.

gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.feature: analysis_h5.write_labels preset/axis params (preset, frame_dim/track_dim/node_dim/xy_dim) + matlab default
gaps.description: Python `save_analysis_h5`/`write_labels` and JS `writeLabels` accept `preset` ("matlab" default → tracks shape (n_tracks,2,n_nodes,n_frames); "standard" → (n_frames,...)) OR explicit frame_dim/track_dim/node_dim/xy_dim positions (mutually exclusive, validated as a permutation of 0..3), via `_get_axis_order`/`getAxisOrder` and `_get_transpose_axes`. Swift writes a single fixed canonical layout with no transpose support and no `dims`/`preset`/`format`/`sleap_io_version` attributes.
gaps.notes: MATLAB-compat ordering is the DEFAULT in upstream; Swift's default is incompatible. Needs nd-array transpose helper (cf. JS transposeFlat).
gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.feature: analysis_h5 track_occupancy MATLAB quirk + dims attribute on every dataset
gaps.swiftLocation: AnalysisHDF5Codec.write — writes track_occupancy as (T,N) uint8, no attrs
gaps.description: Under the matlab preset, `track_occupancy` is intentionally stored (frame,track) while all other 2D arrays are stored (track,frame); every dataset carries a `dims` JSON attribute. Swift writes occupancy as uint8 (T,N) with no `dims` and no preset awareness, so even the occupancy axis convention diverges.
gaps.notes: Small once the preset machinery exists; called out separately because it is an easy-to-miss compatibility quirk.
gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.feature: to_analysis_arrays / to_numpy untracked slotting (_max_instances_per_frame, _untracked_frame_instances, _tracked_frame_instances) + min_occupancy filtering + all_frames
gaps.description: Python `to_analysis_arrays` (and JS `toAnalysisArrays`) build canonical arrays with: first/last frame from actual frame_idx, all_frames flag, untracked-vs-tracked slotting (one instance per track; for untracked, max instances/frame with from_predicted + same-track dedup and single-instance handling), and min_occupancy track filtering with track-name resizing. Swift's writer slots untracked instances by raw per-frame enumeration index and has no min_occupancy/all_frames/from_predicted logic. TensorCodec.toTensor additionally indexes frames by store POSITION (0..<count) not frame_idx, and dumps every untracked instance into slot 0 (overwriting).
gaps.notes: Backend tensor export (sleap.swift) depends on this matching numpy semantics. Swift has no `to_numpy(untracked:)` equivalent at all.
gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.feature: analysis_h5 extended round-trip metadata: skeleton_name, skeleton_symmetries, video_backend_metadata, provenance, labels_path, video_ind
gaps.swiftLocation: AnalysisHDF5Codec.write — writes only video_path attr + edge_inds/edge_names
gaps.description: Python/JS persist `skeleton_name`, `skeleton_symmetries` (JSON), `video_backend_metadata` (JSON) as file attrs and `provenance`, `labels_path`, `video_ind` as datasets (save_metadata flag), and on read rebuild skeleton symmetries + video backend metadata. Swift writes only `video_path` and edges; it drops symmetries, provenance, labels_path, video_ind, and never restores symmetries/backend metadata on read.
gaps.notes: Symmetries matter for a labeling GUI (symmetric-node UI); provenance round-trip matters for project fidelity.
gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.description: Python `is_analysis_h5_file` / JS `isAnalysisH5File` open the HDF5 and return true iff a `track_occupancy` dataset is present, distinguishing analysis files from JABS `poseest` files. Swift has no such detector, so a generic loader cannot route .h5 files between analysis and JABS readers.
gaps.notes: Needed for any `load(path)` dispatch in a GUI that accepts mixed .h5 inputs.
gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.feature: JABS pose-version model (v2 single-mouse 3D, v3 instance_track_id+instance_count, v4+ instance_embed_id) + version attr on poseest
gaps.description: Python `read_labels`/JS `loadJabs` branch on the `poseest.version` attribute: v2 reads single-mouse (F,N,2)→one Track("1"); v3 reads `instance_track_id` + `instance_count`; v4+ reads `instance_embed_id`, skipping ids<=0. Swift ignores version entirely, requires a 4D points array plus a `node_names` root attribute that real JABS files do NOT have, and builds tracks named `animal_N` by slot index. Swift cannot read any standard JABS pose file.
gaps.notes: Real JABS files have no node_names attr — they rely on the built-in Mouse skeleton — so Swift's read path throws on genuine input.
gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.feature: JABS default Mouse skeleton (12 keypoints, JABS_DEFAULT_EDGES, JABS_DEFAULT_SYMMETRIES) + make_simple_skeleton
gaps.swiftLocation: JABSCodec — uses Skeleton(name:"JABS") from file node_names only
gaps.description: Python/JS define the canonical 12-node JABS Mouse skeleton (NOSE..TIP_TAIL) with 11 edges and 3 symmetries (ears, front paws, rear paws) used as the default when reading, plus `make_simple_skeleton(name,n)` building a linear-chain skeleton. Swift has neither; it only constructs an edgeless skeleton from a (nonexistent) file attribute.
gaps.notes: Without the default skeleton, edges/symmetries are lost on JABS import, degrading skeleton overlays in a GUI.
gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.feature: JABS y/x coordinate flip on read and write
gaps.description: JABS stores keypoints as (y,x); Python `np.flip(..., axis=-1)` and JS swap to (x,y) on read and back to (y,x) on write. Swift reads `pointsFlat[...*2]`→x, `+1`→y with no flip, so any real JABS file would be transposed (x/y swapped). Combined with the format mismatch this means coordinates are wrong even if the shape happened to match.
gaps.notes: Silent correctness bug for any genuinely-JABS input.
gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.feature: JABS write versions write_jabs_v2/v3/v4/v5 + tracklets_to_v3 + per-video file naming (_pose_est_vN.h5)
gaps.swiftLocation: JABSCodec.write — single generic (T,N,K,2) layout + node_names attr

JS deliberately omits the writer. Swift writes one ad-hoc layout with a `node_names` attr that real JABS readers don't expect; no version param, no identity datasets, no tracklet normalization, no per-video naming.
gaps.notes: Python explicitly supports only v2-v5 write. JS skips writer by design (issue #99: one-time JABS→SLP is the common path). For an Apple GUI, JABS export is low priority; mark low.
gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.feature: JABS static objects (v5+) as UserROI (corners→arena, others→anchor, source="jabs") + _static_object_to_roi / _roi_to_static_object_coords
gaps.description: Python/JS read `static_objects/<name>` keypoint arrays into UserROI (Point/MultiPoint geometry; category "arena" for corners else "anchor"; source "jabs") and Python writes them back in v5. Swift reads none of this and has no ROI model wired into JABS.
gaps.notes: Depends on a Swift ROI model existing; out of scope until ROIs land. GUI relevance low for mouse-arena anchors.
gaps.module: DLC / JABS / Ultralytics-YOLO / Analysis-HDF5 import-export

gaps.feature: JABS get_max_ids_in_video / convert_labels skeleton-name=='Mouse' filtering + unassigned-track ID fallback warnings

Swift's writer throws on multi-instance untracked frames and has no Mouse-skeleton selection or fallback-ID logic.
gaps.notes: Writer-only nicety; low priority for Apple port.

gaps.swiftLocation: DLCCodec.read — reads pandas HDFStore `df_with_missing` HDF5 instead of CSV
gaps.description: Python `load_dlc` reads DeepLabCut annotation CSVs (scorer/bodyparts/coords or individuals/bodyparts/coords multi-level headers, MultiIndex image paths, frame index from filename) and builds per-video image-sequence Videos. JS has no DLC support at all. Swift builds only an edgeless `DLC` skeleton from columns and has no config/project/crop/source-video machinery.

gaps.description: Read/write a GeoJSON FeatureCollection (RFC 7946) where each Feature is one ROI. read_rois accepts both a FeatureCollection and a single bare Feature, skips Features with null geometry, and pulls name/category/source from properties into a UserROI. write_rois dumps a FeatureCollection with indent=2. JS mirrors this exactly with string and object variants.
gaps.notes: Both Python and JS implement this, so it is firmly in scope for parity. Swift can do all of this with Foundation JSONSerialization/Codable (no native dependency). The real blocker is the geometry model gap below — Swift's ROI has no Polygon/MultiPolygon geometry to serialize round-trip.
gaps.module: io/{geojson, trackmate, seq, tiff, nwb, nwb_annotations, nwb_predictions, leap}

gaps.description: Python ROI wraps a real Shapely geometry (Polygon, box, Point, MultiPolygon) and exposes __geo_interface__ producing a GeoJSON Feature dict (geometry + properties). JS ROI exposes toGeoJSON()/fromGeoJSON. Swift ROI instead stores a flat [SIMD2<Float>] coordinate list with an AnnotationType enum and ad-hoc point-in-polygon; it has no nested-ring Polygon, no MultiPolygon, no holes, and no GeoJSON geometry serialization.
gaps.notes: This is the load-bearing gap for GeoJSON parity. To round-trip GeoJSON you need a Swift geometry enum (Point/Polygon-with-holes/MultiPolygon) plus a coordinates encoder. A SwiftUI annotation GUI editing polygonal ROIs would benefit, but most SLEAP annotation is keypoint-based, so medium not high.
gaps.module: io/{geojson, trackmate, seq, tiff, nwb, nwb_annotations, nwb_predictions, leap}

Swift ROI only has boundingBox (CGRect) and a contains() point test; no area, no centroid, no is_bbox detection, no multipolygon constructor.
gaps.notes: Needed both for GeoJSON fidelity and for any ROI editing/measurement UI. area/centroid/bounds are straightforward over a polygon; is_bbox is a small ring-shape check.

gaps.module: io/{geojson, trackmate, seq, tiff, nwb, nwb_annotations, nwb_predictions, leap}

Handles TCYX series and per-class binary-mask stacks via from_binary_masks with label-ID inference.

gaps.module: io/{geojson, trackmate, seq, tiff, nwb, nwb_annotations, nwb_predictions, leap}

gaps.feature: to_numpy / Labels.numpy() frame-axis alignment (n_frames = last_frame - first_frame + 1, spans video length)
gaps.description: Python to_numpy sizes axis 0 as last_frame-first_frame+1 and indexes each frame at i = frame_idx - first_frame, also extending to video length (len(video)) so output spans the whole clip. Swift uses frameStore.count for frameCount and writes at the frameStore position (frameIdx loop var), so output is keyed by stored-frame position, not real frame_idx. For sparse/labeled-only stores this misaligns every instance with its true video frame and produces wrong-length arrays. JS toNumpy delegates to labels.numpy with numFrames/video.shape fallback.
gaps.notes: This is the core training/analysis array; the misalignment is a real correctness bug for any sparse Labels. No first_frame return value either.
gaps.module: Codecs: DictionaryCodec + TensorCodec (numpy/tensor export, dataframe export, skeleton YAML, training-config parsing)

gaps.description: Python _untracked_frame_instances + _max_instances_per_frame size the track axis to the max per-frame instance count and slot each untracked instance into a distinct positional slot j. Swift forces every track-less instance into trackIdx=0, so multiple untracked instances in one frame overwrite each other (only the last survives) and trackCount is max(tracks.count,1) which is 1 for trackless multi-animal data — silently dropping animals. Also missing the user/predicted dedup (from_predicted / shared-track preference) and is_single_instance handling.
gaps.notes: Critical for trackless prediction output and DLC-style imports. Python keeps all instances; Swift loses data.

Swift toTensor only has includeScores (≈return_confidence) and no video filter, no user/predicted toggles, no untracked flag — it always uses all frames and all instances. JS toNumpy supports video and numFrames but not the user/predicted/untracked flags either.
gaps.notes: Backend needs video filtering + user/predicted selection to reproduce SLEAP analysis exports.
gaps.module: Codecs: DictionaryCodec + TensorCodec (numpy/tensor export, dataframe export, skeleton YAML, training-config parsing)

gaps.description: Python from_numpy and JS fromNumpy/labelsFromNumpy reconstruct a Labels from a (n_frames,n_tracks,n_nodes,2|3) array: auto-create tracks (track_names or track_i defaults), build PredictedInstance.from_numpy per non-NaN slot, skip empty frames/tracks, fix NaN scores to 1.0, honor first_frame, validate video/videos and skeleton/skeletons mutual-exclusion. Swift has no inverse of toTensor at all.
gaps.notes: Inference backend produces these arrays and must turn them back into Labels for saving .slp / overlays.
gaps.module: Codecs: DictionaryCodec + TensorCodec (numpy/tensor export, dataframe export, skeleton YAML, training-config parsing)

Swift exposes only raw PointsArray.coordinates and PredictedPointsArray.scores; there is no per-instance numpy()/array accessor that returns NaN for invisible points the way Python does, so callers must hand-roll the NaN masking each time.

gaps.module: Codecs: DictionaryCodec + TensorCodec (numpy/tensor export, dataframe export, skeleton YAML, training-config parsing)

gaps.swiftLocation: AnalysisHDF5Codec.write (Sources/SleapHDF5/AnalysisHDF5Codec.swift:249) reimplements a subset; no SleapIO-level builder
gaps.description: Python codecs.numpy.to_analysis_arrays is a reusable builder returning all five matrices plus track_names and first_frame, with min_occupancy filtering, all_frames toggle, untracked positional slotting reusing to_numpy logic, and synthetic track_0..track_n names. Swift only has an inlined partial version inside SleapHDF5.AnalysisHDF5Codec.write: it lacks min_occupancy filtering, the all_frames=False (first labeled frame) option, and the empty/low-occupancy track pruning; it also enforces single-video/single-skeleton limits Python does not. There is no standalone SleapIO API a backend can call to get the arrays without writing a file.

gaps.module: Codecs: DictionaryCodec + TensorCodec (numpy/tensor export, dataframe export, skeleton YAML, training-config parsing)

gaps.feature: Dictionary format key/shape compatibility with canonical to_dict (labeled_frames, video_idx, skeleton_idx, index-based edges/symmetries, version 1.0.0)
gaps.description: Python/JS to_dict emit a documented, JSON-portable schema: top-level keys skeletons/videos/tracks/labeled_frames/suggestions/provenance/version; skeleton edges as [srcIdx,dstIdx] index pairs and symmetries as sorted index pairs; per-instance skeleton_idx/track_idx, type 'instance'|'predicted_instance', has_from_predicted flag. Swift uses different keys (frames not labeled_frames; per-frame 'video'/'skeleton'/'track' integer fields; type 'user'|'predicted') and serializes skeletons as nested {name} node dicts and {source,destination} name-based edge dicts rather than index pairs, plus a non-standard video backend_type/original_filename. The Swift dict round-trips with itself but is NOT interchangeable with Python/JS JSON, defeating the codec's interop purpose.
gaps.notes: If a SwiftUI GUI ever loads/saves JSON projects shared with the Python ecosystem, the schema mismatch breaks interop. Aligning keys is the main fix.

criticModule.module: Cross-cutting / missed-coverage gaps (public API surface, async/concurrency, provenance, version migration, camera math, remote I/O, Swift-GUI/backend-specific)
criticModule.summary: The per-module audit was thorough on feature surfaces but systematically skipped cross-cutting infrastructure that spans modules. The biggest blind spots: (1) the canonical public API export contract — Python's __init__.py exposes ~120 flat top-level symbols (load_*/save_*, every model class, every matcher) that downstream code imports as `sleap_io.X`, and JS mirrors most via barrel exports; the Swift port has no umbrella/re-export module or documented public surface, so consumers must reach into nested namespaces. (2) Provenance is typed `dict[str, Any]` upstream (values can be ints/floats/lists/nested dicts, e.g. `provenance["cellpose_diameter"] = 30`) but `[String: String]` in Swift — a silent data-loss/round-trip-corruption bug, not just a feature gap. (3) The multi-camera calibration math (rodrigues_transformation, extrinsic_matrix composition, CameraGroup, the rvec/tvec attrs validation, FrameGroup/InstanceGroup 3D point aggregation) is barely covered — the audit only noted session serialization schema mismatch. (4) Remote/URL/Google-Drive loading (io/_remote.py ~1029 LOC, io/_gdrive.py ~521 LOC) with magic-byte sniffing, HTTP range requests, retry/backoff, and RemoteIOError is entirely absent and was only mentioned in passing. (5) io/utils.py HDF5 helpers, version.py/__version__, format version-migration write path (Swift can read 1.0-1.5 but always writes one fixed version with no migration/downgrade), and async/Sendable/actor-isolation contracts for a SwiftUI @MainActor GUI were not audited as cross-cutting concerns. GUI-critical additions: a public observable/diffable model layer (Swift classes are @unchecked Sendable mutable refs with no Combine/Observation conformance, no change notification, no undo/redo), and stable identity/equality/hashing for SwiftUI ForEach/Identifiable.
